analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare drug plans and PBMs from excluding any willing pharmacy that meets reasonable contract terms from their networks.
analysis.headline: The NO PBMs Act never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from July 2023 until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends Medicare law to require drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers to let any pharmacy that meets their standard contract terms join the plan's network. It also directs CMS to set standards ensuring those contract terms are reasonable, so PBMs cannot use impossible terms to keep local pharmacies out. The goal is to protect seniors' access to the pharmacy of their choice instead of being steered to mail-order or PBM-owned pharmacies.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who want to fill prescriptions at a local, independent, or preferred neighborhood pharmacy rather than a mail-order service or a small PBM-owned network. Independent and community pharmacies also benefit, because they gain guaranteed entry to Medicare drug plan networks if they meet standard contract terms.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare prescription drug plans and the PBMs that build their pharmacy networks to accept any willing pharmacy that meets the plan's contract terms [S2].
Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services (through CMS) to set standards ensuring those contract terms are 'reasonable and relevant' by January 1, 2026 [S3].

The bill's stated purpose is to 'assure pharmacy access and choice for Medicare beneficiaries,' meaning seniors could keep filling prescriptions at their local or preferred pharmacy rather than a mail-order or chain pharmacy the plan picks [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plan sponsors, which would lose their current ability to exclude pharmacies and steer patients toward preferred or affiliated pharmacies. Some of the cost could flow to Medicare premiums if networks must include more pharmacies.

drawbacks.text: The bill's practical benefit depends entirely on CMS writing 'reasonable and relevant' contract standards by January 1, 2026; until standards exist, plans could keep the status quo by keeping their own terms formally open but practically restrictive [S3].

Requiring plans to accept any pharmacy meeting contract terms could raise drug plan costs if plans lose the ability to steer volume to a small set of low-cost pharmacies, and those costs could be passed on in Medicare premiums [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—more pharmacies and more choice for Medicare beneficiaries—is real but narrow, applying only to Medicare drug plans and leaving enforcement details to future CMS standards. The cost is that plans and PBMs might see somewhat higher pharmacy reimbursement baked into networks. The larger weakness is that the bill never got any consideration, so its merits were never weighed or improved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2023 and stayed there until the two-year Congress ended, never reaching a vote.

narrative.text: Introduced in the Senate on July 20, 2023, and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance [S1].
The committee took no further action: no hearings, no markup, and no committee vote appear in the action history [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the large insurers whose plans they manage, who keep their current power to decide which pharmacies seniors may use without any new restrictions.

for.name: Sen. Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the bill's only cosponsor [S3].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no markup or vote ever occurred [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, but with only two senators involved and no votes, no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.note: PBMs currently build Medicare drug plan networks and use that leverage to steer patients to pharmacies they own or favor; the bill would force them to admit any qualifying pharmacy, weakening that control [S2].
Local pharmacies gain guaranteed access to Medicare plan networks if they meet standard contract terms, instead of being squeezed out by PBM networks and affiliated pharmacies [S2].
Plans would lose network flexibility and could face higher pharmacy reimbursement costs, but the requirement applies only within Medicare's Part D program.
